name: Vedanta
line: Inquire into the self behind experience.

quote.text: Tat tvam asi: that thou art.

quotes.text: Lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to immortality.
You have a right to your actions, but never to the fruits of your actions.
Arise, awake, and having reached the great teachers, learn.
Brahman is real, the world is appearance, and the self is nothing other than Brahman.
Your own Self-realization is the greatest service you can render the world.

words.usage: Not the personality: the awareness in which the personality appears.
The one, limitless ground of everything. Not the god Brahmā.
The non-dual school: self and reality are one.
Both the last part of the scriptures, the Upaniṣads, and their final meaning.
Teachings given by a teacher to a student sitting close.
One of the four "great sayings". Uddālaka says it to his son nine times.
The great saying of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
The method of setting aside everything that can be observed, to find the observer.
Not illusion as nothing, but mistaking: seeing a snake where there is a rope.
Not knowing what you are. The root of bondage.
Freedom from the sense of being a limited, separate self.

words.meaning: Discrimination between the real and the unreal
words.usage: First of the four qualifications of a student.
Losing the conviction that things will complete you.
The fourth qualification, and the one that drives the rest.
Not three qualities but one nature seen three ways.
Awareness that observes thoughts without being a thought.
The awareness underlying waking, dream and deep sleep.
Direct recognition, not information.
Hearing the teaching. The first of three steps.
Thinking it through until doubt is gone.
Dwelling in what has been understood until it is steady.
Acting fully and offering the result.
Love directed to the divine. A path in its own right.
Work done for others with no claim on the outcome.
A-U-M and the silence after: waking, dream, deep sleep and the fourth.
Chanted three times to close a recitation.
Traditionally explained as the one who removes darkness.
Gathering with a teacher or with others on the path.
Whatever you do daily to steady the mind.
In thought, word and deed.
One of three qualities of nature, with restlessness and inertia.
Said with palms together at the heart.

practices.name: Om chanting
practices.instructions: Sit upright, close your eyes and take three slow breaths. On each long out-breath sound Om in three parts: A, open, from the belly; U, rolling forward through the mouth; M, humming at the lips. Then stay in the silence that follows for as long as the in-breath lasts. Continue for ten minutes. In the last minute, drop the sound and listen only to the silence.
practices.why: The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad is twelve verses on this one syllable. The three sounds stand for waking, dream and deep sleep, and the silence for the awareness that is present in all three.
variations: Chant silently, hearing it in the mind.
Chant along with a tanpura drone.
End with Om śānti śānti śānti.

practices.name: Self-inquiry: Who am I?
practices.instructions: Sit quietly. When a thought arises, do not follow it. Ask instead: to whom has this thought come? The answer is "to me". Then ask: who am I? Do not answer in words. Turn attention back toward the sense of "I" itself and rest there. When another thought comes, repeat. The question is not a mantra. It is a way of turning the mind around.
practices.why: Ramana Maharshi taught this as the most direct means: find the source of the "I"-thought and every other thought subsides with it.
variations: Neti neti: I am aware of the body, so I am not the body; of this thought, so not this thought. What remains?
Sit as the witness and simply watch.
Ask the question once in the middle of a busy moment.

practices.name: Study of a verse
practices.instructions: Take one verse of the Bhagavad Gītā or an Upaniṣad. Read it aloud. Read a commentary if you have one. Then close the book and reflect: what does it claim? Is it true in my experience? What would change if I took it seriously? Write one sentence in your own words.
practices.why: The traditional method is three steps: listening, reflecting and contemplating. Study here is not scholarship. It is using words as a mirror.
variations: Read the same verse for a whole week.

practices.name: Karma yoga: service
practices.instructions: Do one piece of work for someone else: cook, clean, help, give. Do it as well as you can. Before you begin, offer it; when it is done, let go of how it is received. Do not mention it.
practices.why: The Gītā’s teaching on action: you have a claim on the work, never on its fruits. Action done without clutching at results purifies the mind and makes it fit for knowledge.
variations: Do an ordinary chore as an offering.
Do your paid work today with full care and no thought of credit.

tasks.name: Read three verses of the Gita

rules.why: The hour and a half before sunrise is called brahma muhūrta, the time of Brahman, when the mind is naturally quiet.
Gītā 2.47. Do the work completely and hand over the outcome.
A sattvic diet, fresh, light and non-violent, is held to keep the mind clear. Follow it as far as your health allows.

rules.text: Do one act of service, unnoticed
rules.why: Service thins the sense of a separate doer.

rules.text: Speak what is true and pleasant
rules.why: Gītā 17.15: speech that causes no distress, that is truthful, agreeable and beneficial.
When disturbed, turn from the cause to the one who is disturbed.

customs.creator: Prasāda

ethics.title: Non-harming
ethics.text: Ahiṃsā. If one self looks out through every pair of eyes, to harm another is to harm yourself.
ethics.practice: Go through today without a single cutting remark.

ethics.title: Act without clinging to fruits
ethics.text: Do what is yours to do, fully, and release the result. Anxiety about outcomes belongs to the sense of being the doer.
ethics.practice: Choose one task and do it for its own sake.

ethics.title: See the self in all beings
ethics.text: Īśā Upaniṣad: one who sees all beings in the self and the self in all beings does not shrink from anyone.
ethics.practice: With each person today, silently note: the same awareness.

ethics.title: Truthfulness
ethics.text: Satya. The pursuit of what is real begins with not lying.
ethics.practice: Catch one small exaggeration before you make it.

ethics.title: Contentment
ethics.text: Santoṣa: being at ease with what is present, while still doing your work.
ethics.practice: Before bed, name three things that were sufficient.

ethics.title: Self-restraint
ethics.text: The Gītā calls the mind restless and hard to curb, and says it can be trained by practice and dispassion.
ethics.practice: Decline one indulgence today, kindly and without drama.

philosophy.title: Ātman is Brahman
philosophy.text: The awareness reading these words and the ground of the whole universe are not two things. This is the central claim of Advaita.
philosophy.practice: Sit for a minute as plain awareness, before any description of yourself.

philosophy.title: The world as appearance
philosophy.text: In dim light a rope is taken for a snake. The fear is real; the snake never was. So the many are seen where there is only the one.
philosophy.practice: Notice one thing today you feared that turned out to be a rope.

philosophy.title: The witness
philosophy.text: You see the body, so you are not only the body. You know your thoughts, so you are not only your thoughts. What is it that knows?
philosophy.practice: When a mood comes, say: I am aware of this mood.

philosophy.title: Four aids
philosophy.text: Discrimination, dispassion, the six disciplines of calm and self-control, and the longing for freedom: what a student needs to bring.
philosophy.practice: Which of the four is weakest in you? Work on that one today.

philosophy.title: Three states
philosophy.text: Waking, dreaming and deep sleep come and go. Something is present through all three, or you could not say "I slept well".
philosophy.practice: On waking tomorrow, notice the moment before the day’s story starts.

philosophy.title: Not this, not this
philosophy.text: Whatever you can point to is an object, and you are the one to whom it appears. Set each aside and see what cannot be set aside.
philosophy.practice: Try it for five minutes: body, breath, feelings, thoughts. What is left?

philosophy.title: Action and knowledge
philosophy.text: Action cannot produce what is already the case. It can only clear the mind so the fact is recognised.
philosophy.practice: Do your service today as preparation, not as achievement.

philosophy.title: The one and the many
philosophy.text: Gold is made into many ornaments and remains gold. Names and forms differ; the substance is one.
philosophy.practice: Look at three very different people and find what is identical.

philosophy.title: Bliss is your nature
philosophy.text: Happiness is not brought in from outside. It is what remains when wanting pauses.
philosophy.practice: Notice the quiet contentment just after a desire is met. Where did it come from?

philosophy.title: Liberation while living
philosophy.text: Freedom is not after death or elsewhere. The jīvanmukta lives an ordinary life with no sense of being bound.
philosophy.practice: Ask once today: what, right now, is actually binding me?

journal: Who was aware of your thoughts today?
Where did you act without needing a result?
What did you take yourself to be today: body, role, or something else?
What did silence show you?
What did you chase today, and did it deliver?
When did you feel most yourself, and what were you not doing?
What rope did you take for a snake?
What did the verse you studied say to you?
Where did you want credit for your service?
What disturbed you, and who was disturbed?
What changed today, and what did not change?
When did happiness appear without a cause?
What were you attached to this morning that seems smaller tonight?
In whom did you fail to see yourself?
What happened when you asked "Who am I?"
What did you say that was not quite true?
What would you do tomorrow if success and failure were the same to you?
What do you believe you lack?
Describe the moment between two thoughts.
What did you eat, and how did it leave your mind?
Which role did you play today as if it were all of you?
What were you the witness of?
What did the sound of Om leave behind?
Where did you harm, even slightly?
What is the same in you now as when you were a child?
What do you want most? What do you want that for?
What did you offer today?
Which doubt is still alive?
What does freedom mean to you tonight?
What remains when today is set aside?

Which practice changed you the most, and why?
Where did you resist, and what was the resistance protecting?
How has your relationship to results changed?
What do you no longer need in order to be at peace?

intro: Vedānta is the philosophical heart of the Hindu tradition. Its question is the plainest one there is: what am I? Its answer, in the non-dual school this Onda follows, is that the self behind your experience and the reality behind the universe are one and the same.

The word means "the end of the Vedas". The Vedas are India’s oldest scriptures, and their closing sections, the Upaniṣads, turn from ritual to inquiry. Composed from around 800 BCE onward, they record teachers and students in forest retreats pressing toward what is ultimately real. They call it Brahman. They call the innermost self Ātman. And in a handful of short sentences, the "great sayings", they declare the two identical: tat tvam asi, that thou art.

Two later texts complete the foundation. The Bhagavad Gītā, a dialogue between the warrior Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna on the eve of battle, teaches how to act in the world without being bound by it. The Brahma Sūtras organise the Upaniṣads’ teaching into terse aphorisms. Every school of Vedānta is, formally, a commentary on these three.

They do not agree. Śaṅkara, who lived around the eighth century, argued for Advaita, "not two": only Brahman is real, the world of separate things is an appearance, like a rope mistaken for a snake, and liberation is the direct knowledge that you were never a limited self. Rāmānuja, three centuries later, held that selves and the world are real, as the body of a personal God. Madhva insisted on an eternal difference between God and the soul. Devotional India largely followed the last two. Advaita became the tradition’s best-known philosophy.

Its method is knowledge, not belief. A student listens to the teaching, reflects until doubts are resolved, and contemplates until the understanding is steady. Ethical life and selfless action prepare the mind. In the twentieth century the sage Ramana Maharshi distilled the whole path into one practice: ask "Who am I?" and follow the sense of "I" back to its source.

This Onda combines the Gītā’s yoga of action with Advaita’s inquiry: chant, ask, study, serve. Vedānta lives within Hindu religious life and its lineages of teachers. If the inquiry deepens, the tradition’s own advice is to find one.

figures.name: Yājñavalkya
figures.bio: Sage of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. Teaches "not this, not this" to his wife Maitreyī and King Janaka.

figures.name: Uddālaka Āruṇi
figures.bio: Teaches his son Śvetaketu "that thou art" with salt dissolved in water.

figures.name: Bādarāyaṇa
figures.bio: Credited with the Brahma Sūtras, the systematic text of Vedānta.

figures.name: Gauḍapāda
figures.bio: Author of the verses on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad. Teacher of Śaṅkara’s teacher.

figures.name: Śaṅkara
figures.bio: The great expounder of Advaita. Wrote the classic commentaries and by tradition founded four monasteries across India.

figures.name: Rāmānuja
figures.bio: Founder of qualified non-dualism, in which devotion to a personal God is central.

figures.name: Ramakrishna
figures.bio: Bengali mystic who practiced several religions and declared them paths to one truth.

figures.name: Swami Vivekananda
figures.bio: Ramakrishna’s disciple. Brought Vedānta to the West in 1893.

figures.name: Ramana Maharshi
figures.bio: Sage of Arunachala. Taught self-inquiry, mostly through silence.

history.detail: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya are the oldest. They move the focus of Vedic religion from sacrifice to knowledge of the self.
Set within the epic Mahābhārata, it gathers the paths of action, knowledge and devotion into one teaching.
Some 555 aphorisms attributed to Bādarāyaṇa, so compressed that they cannot be read without a commentary.
The first systematic statement of non-dualism, analysing waking, dream and sleep.
In a short life he writes commentaries on the three foundational texts, debates rivals across India and, by tradition, founds monasteries at Sringeri, Dwarka, Puri and Jyotirmath.
His Śrī Bhāṣya defends a real world and a personal God and gives the devotional movements a philosophy.
God, souls and matter are eternally distinct.

history.what: The Upaniṣads are translated into Persian
history.detail: The Mughal prince Dara Shikoh has fifty of them rendered as "The Great Secret". A Latin version of 1801–02 reaches Schopenhauer, who calls it the consolation of his life.
Charles Wilkins’s translation is read by Emerson and Thoreau in New England.

At the World’s Parliament of Religions he opens with "Sisters and brothers of America" and receives a long ovation. He founds the Vedanta Society in New York the next year and the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897.
At sixteen, seized by a fear of death, he lies down and inquires into what dies. Weeks later he leaves home for the hill of Arunachala and stays for life.

The Republic of India adopts "Truth alone triumphs", from the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, as its national motto. In the same years teachers such as Swami Chinmayananda begin teaching Vedānta publicly in English.
The dialogues of Nisargadatta Maharaj reach a worldwide audience.

concepts.detail: Described only by negation, or as being-consciousness-bliss. It is not a thing among things and not a creator standing apart from creation.

concepts.text: The self that is pure awareness.
concepts.detail: Not the ego or the personality, which are objects of awareness. The Upaniṣads call it the seer of seeing, the hearer of hearing.

concepts.text: The power by which the one appears as many.
concepts.detail: Śaṅkara calls the world neither real nor unreal: it is experienced, so not nothing; it is cancelled by knowledge, so not final.
Adhyāsa: the properties of the body and mind are projected onto the self, and the self’s reality onto them. All bondage is this mix-up.

concepts.text: Four sentences that state the identity of self and Brahman.
concepts.detail: Consciousness is Brahman; I am Brahman; that thou art; this self is Brahman. One from each of the four Vedas.
Each cancels the others, yet awareness persists through all. That persisting awareness is called the fourth, turīya.
Karma yoga purifies the mind, bhakti steadies and sweetens it, and jñāna removes ignorance. Advaita holds knowledge to be the direct means and the others its preparation.
Discrimination, dispassion, a set of six inner disciplines, and an intense wish to be free.
Hear the teaching from a competent teacher, reason through objections, then dwell on what is understood until it is unshakeable.

concepts.text: Mokṣa is knowledge, not an event.
concepts.detail: Nothing new is gained. A wrong idea about oneself is dropped. One who has dropped it while alive is called jīvanmukta, liberated in life.

facts.text: Upaniṣad is usually explained as "sitting down near": the teaching was given at close quarters, one to one.
More than a hundred Upaniṣads exist. Ten to thirteen are treated as principal, and Śaṅkara commented on these.
The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad is only twelve verses long. A traditional saying holds that it alone is enough for liberation.
Schopenhauer kept a Latin translation of the Upaniṣads at his bedside.
Robert Oppenheimer learned Sanskrit to read the Gītā and quoted it after the first atomic test.
Ramana Maharshi spent years in near-total silence. Many visitors said the silence taught them more than his words.
The syllable Oṃ is analysed as A, U, M and a fourth soundless part, matching waking, dream, sleep and pure awareness.
Śaṅkara is traditionally said to have died at thirty-two.

glossary.meaning: The oldest Hindu scriptures. Vedānta is their concluding portion.
The three foundations: Upaniṣads, Brahma Sūtras and Bhagavad Gītā.
A place of spiritual retreat and teaching.

sensitivity.note: Vedānta is part of living Hindu tradition and is normally learned from a teacher within a lineage. This Onda introduces its texts and its most widely taught practices.
requiredCaveats: A vegetarian diet is traditional, not required: adapt it to your health.
Self-inquiry can be unsettling. If it becomes distressing, pause and return to chanting, study and service.
